ai-agent: A clear editorial-style illustration of an AI agent as a small central control desk with a glowing language-model “brain” interpreting a task checklist, then directing visible tool arms toward separate panels: a web browser search, a folder of company files, a code terminal, a document editor, a calendar, and an email inbox; arrows form a loop from plan to action to observed result and back to the plan, showing multi-step decision-making. Around the desk, permissions appear as locked gates and limited-access badges, while high-consequence actions such as sending an email or changing an online account pause at a prominent human confirmation button. A transparent activity log records each step beside a large red stop switch and an undo/correction control, making the contrast between useful autonomy and carefully bounded, accountable action immediately legible.
benchmark: A clear editorial illustration of several different AI systems lined up at the same standardized testing station, each facing identical task cards labeled “repair code,” “write analysis,” “research,” and “use terminal,” while a large scoreboard measures their scores with neat, repeatable rules; behind the station, the scene opens into a messy real workplace where a person presents an ambiguous request, scattered follow-up questions, an existing codebase, and a long chain of interconnected steps, showing that the tidy test captures only part of practical usefulness; in one corner, a model studies a familiar leaked-looking test sheet, while in another, an evaluator combines the benchmark score with independent real-task trials, conveying benchmarks as valuable but incomplete evidence rather than a final verdict.
tokens: A clear editorial infographic shows a large sentence entering a stylized language model as a stream of individually separated pieces—whole short words, broken word fragments, punctuation marks, and small space symbols—each rendered as numbered tiles; inside the model, the tiles become a sequential ribbon, then emerge as a newly generated ribbon of output tiles forming a response. Beneath, a simple cost meter splits into two labeled columns, “input tokens” for the prompt, document, conversation history, agent notes, and tool-call loops flowing in, and “output tokens” for the generated answer flowing out, with both feeding a single larger gauge labeled “cost to complete the task”; visual callouts show how a huge document, long answer, retries, and repeated agent-tool cycles make the gauge rise, while a small comparison chart of per-token rates sits in the background as useful but secondary information.
